conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and to check on how you’ve been feeling lately.  
Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question tool that helps us see whether you might be experiencing postpartum depression or anxiety, and it includes a question about thoughts of self-harm. Your answers are completely confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. We’ll go through one question at a own pace; just tell me how things have been for you over the past seven days.

To start: In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, laughing feels really hard lately. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I just… couldn’t. I stared at it, knew it was supposed to be funny, but nothing came. Most of the time I feel like I’m stuck behind a foggy window watching everyone else enjoy things.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… that doesn’t fit me. I haven’t been able to laugh at all this week. I might force a little smile so people don’t worry, but nothing feels funny inside.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to anything. Even little things I used to enjoy—like my morning coffee or a walk—just feel flat. I still do them, but it’s more going through the motions than feeling any real excitement.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby cries longer than usual, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. I keep replaying every little thing in my head, convinced I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when everything looks fine—he’s sleeping, the house is quiet—I’ll suddenly worry his breathing sounds different or that he’ll choke on spit-up the second I look away. My heart races and I can’t settle unless I check on him every few minutes.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes... it hits out of nowhere. I'll be folding laundry and suddenly feel like the walls are closing in, like something awful is about to happen—maybe to the baby, maybe to me—and my chest gets tight and I can't catch my breath. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Feeding, changing, trying to soothe him when he won’t stop crying—sometimes it piles up so fast I feel like I’m drowning. I’ll sit on the couch with him in my arms and think, “How am I going to get through the next hour?” I still manage the basics, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—worrying I’m not doing enough, replaying every little sound the baby made, imagining worst-case scenarios. Even when he’s asleep, I can’t settle; I’ll toss and turn for hours or wake up at three a.m. and just stare at the ceiling until morning.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I feel that way most of the day. It’s like a heavy blanket I can’t push off. I look at the baby and feel love, but it’s quickly followed by this wave of sadness I can’t explain. Little things make me tear up—seeing other moms who seem to have it together, or when my partner asks how I’m doing. I end up crying a few times a week, usually when I’m alone and the house is finally quiet.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… that’s been me. The sadness just builds until it spills over. A couple of nights ago I was warming up a bottle and suddenly felt like the world was caving in—next thing I knew I was sobbing at the kitchen counter. It happens maybe three or four times a week; sometimes I don’t even know what set me off, just this overwhelming sense that I’m failing and I can’t fix it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… that hasn’t crossed my mind. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

It sounds like you've been carrying a heavy emotional load since your baby arrived. Over the past week you've described feeling unable to laugh or look forward to anything, persistent sadness that brings you to tears several times a week, near-constant worry and sudden episodes of panic, nightly difficulty sleeping, and frequent self-blame about your parenting. These experiences seem overwhelming and exhausting, yet you've also shared that thoughts of harming yourself have not occurred to you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states inability to laugh and finds nothing funny, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities as "flat" and "going through the motions," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, persistent self-blame for routine infant crying, indicating she blames herself "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, excessive worry occurring "pretty much all the time" with intrusive thoughts about infant safety, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('most days'), feeling 'drowning' and 'barely keeping my head above water,' matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty sleeping due to unhappiness, consistent with most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness most of the day, frequent crying spells, and emotional triggers matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense crying episodes 3-4 times per week triggered by overwhelming sadness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 25 places you well above the threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms such as daily low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, disproportionate guilt, and repeated crying, alongside prominent anxiety and panic. Sleep disturbance is directly linked to unhappiness, and you describe feeling unable to cope "most days," fulfilling multiple <med>DSM-5</med> criteria for a depressive episode. Because scores ≥14 warrant urgent assessment, and you scored 25 without endorsing self-harm, immediate referral is recommended to confirm diagnosis and initiate treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Discuss evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>antidepressant medication</med> safe for breastfeeding
3. Plan nightly wind-down routine: low lighting, screen-free time, brief relaxation breathing to improve <sym>sleep onset</sym>
4. Accept practical help from family or friends for housework and night feeds to reduce <sym>stress load</sym>
5. Keep the baby-care checklist simple; aim for "good-enough" rather than perfect to lessen <sym>self-criticism</sym>
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after starting support
7. Maintain safety: if low mood escalates or any thoughts of self-harm emerge, contact your provider or emergency services immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: self-report on 10-item EPDS analogue

Identified symptoms/concerns  
- Marked anhedonia (loss of humor, anticipatory pleasure)  
- Persistent low mood with daily crying spells  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Near-constant free-floating anxiety and episodic panic (tight chest, breathlessness)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed/drowning in daily tasks  
- Mood-related insomnia (initial and middle)  

Pattern  
Symptoms present “most days,” interfere with basic coping, but no self-harm ideation reported.

Screening significance  
Responses are consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with prominent anxiety.  
No current safety risk (denies self-harm); nevertheless, distress level warrants prompt follow-up for formal evaluation and possible intervention.

Next step  
Recommend immediate referral to OB/maternal mental health specialist for structured diagnostic interview and discussion of treatment options.
